name: Interdental brushes

lead: Interdental brushes are small bristled brushes that fit between teeth to clean plaque from spaces a normal toothbrush misses.
Systematic reviews have generally found adding them to toothbrushing is associated with less plaque and gum inflammation, though certainty varies by outcome.

paras: Bristles or elastomer fins are passed through the gap between teeth to physically disrupt plaque on the side surfaces of teeth and along the gum margin.
The research reviewed focuses on efficacy. Brushes sized too large or used forcefully can irritate gums, and sizes are graded by the ISO 16409 standard for that reason.

lead: Interdental brushes are small, bristled brushes, usually on a short handle, designed to pass through the gaps between teeth and around orthodontic hardware to remove plaque from surfaces a regular toothbrush reaches poorly. They are sold over the counter in graded sizes, typically alongside floss, picks and similar devices.[1]

Systematic reviews, including Cochrane reviews, have examined interdental cleaning devices as an addition to toothbrushing for plaque, gum inflammation and tooth decay.[2][3] Researchers generally report that interdental brushing alongside toothbrushing is associated with lower plaque and gingival inflammation than toothbrushing alone, with the certainty of the evidence described as limited for some outcomes.[2][3] Interdental brushes are discussed in looksmaxxing circles mainly in the context of gum health and the look of the gum line.
infobox: ISO 16409 sizes 0 to 8, by gap diameter[1]

paras: Common designs use a twisted wire core holding nylon bristles, or a flexible rubbery elastomer head. The ISO 16409 standard numbers sizes from 0 to 8 according to the diameter of the passage a brush can pass through without bending its wire, from about 0.6 mm at size 0 to 2.8 mm or more at size 8. Colours and wire diameters vary by manufacturer.[1] End-tuft brushes are a separate, related device used for areas such as behind the last molars, around braces and near implants.[1]

A 2008 systematic review assessed interdental brushes as an adjunct to toothbrushing against toothbrushing alone or other interdental devices, looking at plaque and clinical measures of gum inflammation.[3] Two Cochrane reviews, in 2013 and 2019, assessed interdental cleaning for periodontal disease and caries in adults and in general populations.[2][4] A 2018 network meta-analysis and a 2020 review of periodontal maintenance patients compared interproximal methods against one another.[5][6]

Several trials compared brushes with dental floss. A 1991 study measured proximal plaque removal with each device, a 1998 trial in patients with moderate to severe periodontitis used floss on one side of the mouth and brushes on the other for six weeks, and a 2018 randomised trial in young people with intact gum papillae compared several devices.[7][8][9] A narrative review of oral hygiene measures notes that interdental brushes and wooden sticks may offer advantages where gums have receded or periodontal disease is present.[10]

Human trials and systematic reviews have compared interdental brushes with toothbrushing alone and with floss for plaque and gingival measures.[2][3][7][8][9] Summaries of these reviews describe benefits over toothbrushing alone for plaque and gingivitis, and report that conclusions about caries remain uncertain.[2] Brushes have often been reported to perform at least as well as floss in people with open gaps, but the trials differ in design and population.[5][7]

The sources reviewed focus on efficacy rather than harms. General dental guidance notes that forceful cleaning or a brush too large for the space can irritate gums, which is why sizing standards exist.[1]
Interdental brushes appear in appearance-focused oral care as an inexpensive gum-health item. Published research on them addresses periodontal health, not cosmetic outcomes.
